title: Gradually and Then Suddenly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Borrows Hemingway's line about bankruptcy -- 'gradually and then suddenly' -- to describe how leadership derailment, burnout, and toxic culture typically build through accumulated small choices before collapsing all at once. The piece's central diagnosis is that leaders become progressively disconnected from ground truth because status and power filter what team members are willing to tell them, so the 'suddenly' moment is really the delayed arrival of a reality that was visible to everyone else. The remedy is deliberately seeking unfiltered information at the organization's edges -- frontline workers, customers, exiting employees -- rather than waiting for the truth to reach the top on its own.
points: Leadership collapses rarely happen all at once; they accumulate through dozens of small, unaddressed choices during the 'gradual' phase that precedes the visible crisis.
Status and power filter the truth leaders receive, so leaders often believe in a reality that no longer matches what's actually happening.
The corrective is to go directly to unfiltered information at the organization's edges -- frontline staff, customer calls, exit interviews -- rather than waiting for it to be reported upward.
quotes: Leaders generally don’t lose the confidence of their team, reach burnout, or create a toxic culture — among many other outcomes — all at once. These happen slowly over time through dozens or hundreds of small choices, actions, and compromises.
The leadership lesson in “gradually and then suddenly” is essentially about attention.

Because the status, power, and influence wielded by leaders inhibit team members from giving them the unvarnished truth, they often march along believing in a reality that doesn’t match what is really going on.
This false or incomplete sense of reality corrupts how leaders think about the problems and challenges the organization faces, or even what problems exist.
Unfiltered information lives at the edges of the organization—with frontline team members, customers, external experts, and people who have chosen to exit the organization.
